reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: A collection of pus in the peritonsillar space, usually a complication of acute tonsillitis, most common in young adults
Presents with severe unilateral sore throat, progressively worsening odynophagia, fever and marked malaise
Classic signs include trismus, a muffled hot-potato voice, drooling and foul breath
Examination shows a bulging, congested soft palate that displaces the uvula and tonsil toward the opposite side
Management principles include drainage of pus by needle aspiration or incision, together with systemic antibiotics, analgesia and hydration
Interval tonsillectomy is often advised after resolution, particularly with recurrent abscesses or a background of recurrent tonsillitis
Trismus can make examination and airway assessment difficult, so vigilance for airway compromise is essential
Untreated infection can spread to the parapharyngeal space and beyond, risking deep neck infection and airway obstruction
reference.pathophysiology: Peritonsillar abscess develops when infection extends beyond the tonsillar capsule into the loose peritonsillar space between the tonsil and the superior constrictor muscle, typically as a progression of acute tonsillitis or from obstructed minor salivary (Weber) glands. Cellulitis in this space evolves into a localised collection of pus, most often at the upper pole. The expanding abscess pushes the tonsil and soft palate medially, irritates the pterygoid muscles to cause trismus, and can dissect into adjacent deep neck spaces, threatening the airway and vascular structures.
additionalDifferentials: Dental or peritonsillar space infection from another source
additionalInvestigations: Oropharyngeal examination assessing palatal bulge, uvular deviation and trismus
Needle aspiration to confirm and localise pus
Full blood count and inflammatory markers
Contrast CT of the neck when deep neck space extension is suspected or examination is limited
Airway assessment and monitoring in severe cases
redFlags: Signs of airway compromise such as stridor, respiratory distress, severe trismus or drooling requiring urgent airway management
Rapid spread into parapharyngeal or retropharyngeal spaces indicating deep neck infection
Neck swelling, torticollis or signs of vascular involvement
Systemic sepsis or failure to improve after drainage and antibiotics
reference.prognosis: With timely drainage and antibiotics the outlook is good, but delayed treatment can lead to airway obstruction, deep neck space infection, mediastinitis or vascular complications, which carry significant risk.
pitfalls: Underestimating airway risk in a patient with severe trismus and drooling
Treating with antibiotics alone when pus requires drainage
Missing extension into deep neck spaces
Failing to arrange follow-up and consider interval tonsillectomy in recurrent cases
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Drain the pus by needle aspiration or incision and drainage as the key intervention
Give systemic antibiotics covering streptococci and oral anaerobes, such as penicillin with metronidazole or co-amoxiclav
Provide supportive care with analgesia, antipyretics and intravenous fluid rehydration
Consider a short course of corticosteroid to reduce pain, trismus and swelling
Assess and monitor the airway in severe cases and obtain contrast CT of the neck when deep neck space extension is suspected or examination is limited
Offer interval tonsillectomy after resolution, particularly with recurrent abscesses or a background of recurrent tonsillitis
Refer urgently to ENT for failure to improve or for complications such as spreading deep neck infection or airway compromise
